id: DS003
title: GPU and Resources
status: accepted
owner: local-llm
summary: Manifest-declared GPU access and the operator override, admission, runner isolation, and memory estimates.
---

# DS003 GPU and Resources

## Introduction

This specification defines how `local-llm` reaches the GPU, how it decides whether a model fits before downloading anything, and how the runner processes are isolated. It replaces the operator-flag approach of repository DS010 with a grant that Ploinky enforces.

## Core Content

### GPU access through the manifest, with the operator override

The manifest declares `containerSecurity.gpu: true` (Ploinky decision D14), so the agent gets the GPU in any workspace where its repo is installed and the host has a usable NVIDIA GPU, with no host step. When the host prepares the Box (`ploinky start`, `restart`, `update`, `gpu grant`, `gpu revoke`) and the host has a usable NVIDIA GPU, it recreates that workspace's Box with the NVIDIA device nodes (`/dev/nvidia0`, `/dev/nvidiactl`, `/dev/nvidia-uvm`), read-only binds of the driver libraries under `/usr/local/nvidia/lib64` and of `nvidia-smi` under `/usr/local/nvidia/bin`, a hookless CDI spec `ploinky.local/gpu=all`, and a grant marker naming the agent. The operator overrides the manifest on the host: `ploinky gpu revoke --agent local-llms/local-llm` denies it persistently, `ploinky gpu grant --agent local-llms/local-llm` restores it, `ploinky gpu revoke` without `--agent` turns manifest-declared GPU access off for the whole workspace, and `ploinky gpu status` shows each GPU agent with its source (Ploinky `ploinky-box/gpuGrant.mjs`).

The declaration asks for that CDI device and nothing else. Ploinky attaches it only while the Box's marker names the agent and is active, and checks again before every launch. Otherwise the agent still starts, without the device, and Ploinky passes `PLOINKY_GPU_STATUS=unavailable` and `PLOINKY_GPU_REASON`, which says what to run on the host: `ploinky gpu grant --agent local-llms/local-llm` after a revoke, `ploinky start` when the repo was installed after the Box was last prepared, or `ploinky gpu status` on a host without a usable GPU. The hardware snapshot reports that reason, so Settings, `local_llm_overview` and `local_llm_status` show it and every Run is refused as `incompatible` with it; there is no CPU fallback in this release (plan decision D7). The agent therefore never fails to start on a machine without a GPU, which matters because Explorer enables it by default. If the GPU disappears while the agent runs, the hardware snapshot reports it unavailable and every Run is refused as `incompatible`.

### Hardware snapshot

`src/controller/hardware.mjs` reads:

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| GPU name, total, used and free memory, driver | `nvidia-smi --query-gpu` (path `/usr/local/nvidia/bin/nvidia-smi`, overridable by `LOCAL_LLM_NVIDIA_SMI` for tests) |
| Other GPU users | `nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps` |
| Total and available RAM | `/proc/meminfo` |
| Free disk under `/data` | `statfs` |

### Admission

`admit()` in `src/controller/admission.mjs` returns one of three answers, each with a reason and an estimate labelled `isEstimate: true`:

| Answer | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ok` | The deployment fits now. A warning is attached when it needs more than half of the RAM available now. | gpt-oss-20b × llama.cpp at 16k context with 17 expert layers in RAM on a 6 GB GPU |
| `incompatible` | This machine can never run these parameters. The reason names the limit and the parameter to change. | 128k context with every expert on the GPU |
| `insufficient-now` | The hardware is enough, but memory or disk is held by something else at the moment. The reason names the other GPU users. | Ollama holding 4.5 GB of VRAM |

Estimates for llama.cpp come from the model's measured memory profile when the catalog has one (non-expert bytes, expert bytes per layer, KV bytes per token, fixed KV bytes), and from the file size otherwise. The gpt-oss-20b profile was measured on an RTX 3060 Laptop GPU (6 GB); for the default parameters the estimate is 4,851 MiB of GPU memory against 4,817 MiB measured. A 256 MiB GPU margin and a 1 GiB RAM margin are kept free. Admission runs when the overview is built, before a download starts, and again before the runner starts.

`admit()` makes the checks every runner shares (the runner is supported, the model has a source in the runner's format, a GPU is available) and then calls the runner adapter's own policy: `admitLlamaServer` for llama.cpp and ik_llama.cpp (the same memory layout for the same GGUF file), `admitLmStudio` for LM Studio, `admitOllama` for Ollama, `admitVllm` for vLLM, and `admitTabbyApi` for TabbyAPI. A runner the release lists but cannot run is `incompatible` with the reason its adapter gives. A runner this deployment's operator left off (LM Studio without its switch, DS001) is `incompatible` with the switch's reason, before any estimate.

`admitLmStudio` is the llama-server estimate plus 768 MiB of RAM for LM Studio's daemon and workers (about 0.6 GB measured at idle). It can reuse the llama-server model because LM Studio runs the same llama-server and the adapter sets every flag that affects memory. Through LM Studio's SDK it sets the context, parallel slots, unified KV, batch and micro-batch sizes, K and V cache types, flash attention on or off, mmap without mlock, and no context checkpoints. Through the SDK's argument override it sets the exact GPU layers, CPU MoE layers and threads. After each load the controller reads the engine's command line, and any flag that differs (the last value of a repeated flag counts), or an engine other than the pinned 2.41.0, fails the start with `runner_flags`. On the RTX 3060 Laptop, gpt-oss-20b at the llama.cpp runner's settings used 4,776 MiB of GPU memory on LM Studio, the same as on llama.cpp.

`admitVllm` keeps all weights on the GPU unless the admin sets `cpuOffloadGb`, which moves that many GiB of weights to system RAM with a warning that generation becomes much slower. It sizes the KV cache for `maxModelLen` from the model's `kvBytesPerToken` (halved for an fp8 KV cache) and adds 768 MiB for activations, the CUDA context and allocator slack, measured with Qwen3-4B-AWQ. CUDA reports about 94 % of nvidia-smi's total as usable. When weights, KV cache and overhead exceed 90 % of that, the model is `incompatible`; the reason names `maxModelLen`, a smaller model, or the least `cpuOffloadGb` that would fit. The GPU share vLLM gets (`--gpu-memory-utilization`) is the admin's value, or else what is free now less two margins, at most 0.9. If that share or the need exceeds what is free now, the answer is `insufficient-now`, naming the other GPU users. With `cpuOffloadGb` set, the system RAM estimate is (1.81 × the offload + 3.0 GiB) × 1.15. It comes from two runs of gpt-oss-20b with 10 GiB offloaded on the RTX 3060 machine (31 GiB of RAM, its 8 GiB swap already full). On 8080, available memory fell from 23.2 to 2.2 GiB, and `free` showed shared memory grow by about 18.1 GiB (1.81 × the offload: vLLM's pinned copies, more than any single process's RssShmem shows). The engine and API server held about 3.0 GiB more. In the fixture, available memory fell by at least 20.1 GiB before a guard stopped the run. An offload run must leave max(4 GiB, 10 % of RAM) available. When the estimate exceeds the available memory less that floor, the answer is `insufficient-now`; the reason names the estimate, what is available and the floor. When it exceeds total RAM less the floor, `incompatible`. The speed warning stays. On the 31 GiB machine, gpt-oss-20b (at least 9 GiB of offload on 6 GB) therefore needs 26.2 GiB available, so it is refused there in practice. The admission records the floor (`ramFloorBytes`), and the controller keeps a memory guard as the backstop. While such a runner loads, it samples MemAvailable every 2 s, and every 10 s once the runner is ready. If available memory falls below the floor, it stops the runner at once (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL within the drain's 3 s grace), and the deployment ends in `error` with "stopped: host memory below the floor (X GiB available, Y GiB required)". The first estimate (offload + 3 GiB, 13.0 GiB for 10 GiB) admitted a run that took the host down to about 2.2 GiB available with swap full. Without offload, the estimate stays 3 GiB with a 1 GiB margin, and there is no guard.

`admitTabbyApi` keeps all EXL3 weights on the GPU and sizes the KV cache for `cacheSize` tokens (the max sequence length unless set) at the `cacheMode` precision (Q8 a half, Q6 three eighths, Q4 a quarter of FP16), plus an estimated 640 MiB for the CUDA context and one prompt chunk's activations. ExLlamaV3 keeps the model's input embedding (`memory.embeddingBytes`) in system RAM, so that counts toward RAM, not the GPU. It is `incompatible` above the usable share of the GPU or the machine's RAM, and `insufficient-now` above what is free now.

### Runner isolation

| Rule | How |
| --- | --- |
| Loopback only | llama.cpp and ik_llama.cpp get `--host 127.0.0.1`; Ollama gets `OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:<port>` |
| Fixed ports | Each adapter declares its port; `defaultPorts()` refuses two runners on one port. llama.cpp 18080, ik_llama.cpp 18081, vLLM 18082, TabbyAPI 18083, LM Studio 18084 (its daemon also listens on 127.0.0.1:41343, and its engine on a random loopback port), Ollama 18434, all inside the agent's network namespace |
| Not reachable through the Router | `routerAccess.agentPorts: false` closes the agent-port relay for this agent |
| Per-start credentials | llama.cpp and ik_llama.cpp get a fresh random `--api-key` on every start, and vLLM and TabbyAPI a key of their own; the chat responder reads it from the controller. LM Studio has none headless: its server relies on loopback, the agent's own network namespace and the closed relay, and the controller keeps only its own model loaded (DS001) |
| Minimal environment | Runners get `PATH`, `HOME=/data/home`, `LANG` and their own variables only; no agent secrets |
| Reaped on stop and drain | Each runner leads its own process group. Stop sends SIGTERM to the group, then SIGKILL after the grace period; when the runner exits, anything left in its group is killed, so helper processes a runner starts never outlive it |

### Reuse from repository DS010

| DS010 rule | local-llm |
| --- | --- |
| RAM floor checked at startup from a catalog band | Replaced by per-deployment admission against measured or estimated needs |
| GPU passthrough is an operator runtime flag; the manifest cannot express it | Replaced by the manifest declaration `containerSecurity.gpu` with the operator's grant and revoke as override (DS010 Question #1, option 3: manifest field plus operator control) |
| `nvidia-smi` and `/dev/nvidia0` as GPU signals | Kept as the hardware snapshot source, read from the granted paths |
| One loaded model at a time to limit contention | Kept: one deployment at a time; Ollama runs with `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=1` |

## Decisions & Questions

### Question #1: Why is the memory estimate profile-based instead of computed from GGUF metadata?

Response: The GGUF header gives tensor sizes but not the CUDA compute buffers or the runtime's allocation behaviour, which differ by build and flash-attention mode. A profile measured on real hardware and stored with the catalog entry is accurate for the seed model; the file-size heuristic is the fallback for user models and is labelled as such.

## Conclusion

The agent reaches the GPU through its manifest declaration, which the operator can revoke, refuses before downloading when a model cannot fit, keeps runners on loopback behind a per-start key, and never exposes a runner port through the Router.

id: DS004
title: On-demand Runners
status: accepted
owner: local-llm
summary: Runners installed after the image is built, from a lock shipped in the image, a verified cache in /data and a runnable copy rebuilt in the container; a proprietary entry is never downloaded in CI.
---

# DS004 On-demand Runners

## Introduction

llama.cpp, ik_llama.cpp and Ollama are part of the agent image. Heavier runners, the PyTorch-based vLLM and ExLlamaV3 + TabbyAPI, would add several gigabytes to every Explorer deployment, so an administrator installs them only where they are wanted (runners plan, decision R2 = c). This specification defines what may be installed, where the files go, how they are checked, and when the runnable copy is rebuilt.

## Core Content

### What may be installed

The image ships `/opt/local-llm/runners.lock.json` (schema `local-llm.runners-lock/v1`, `src/controller/runnerLock.mjs`). For each installable runner it names the version, the kind (`python` or `archive`), the licence, every file with its URL, size and sha256, and the checks the CI install job runs. Administrators choose a runner id; they never supply a URL. The lock accepts only plain https URLs on `files.pythonhosted.org`, `github.com`, `codeload.github.com`, `download.pytorch.org`, `openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net` and `llmster.lmstudio.ai`, and each file is pinned by size and sha256 as well.

A licence may be marked `proprietary` (LM Studio): the software may not be redistributed, so it never ships in the image, and a proprietary entry must also require acceptance. The CI install check validates such an entry from the lock alone and never downloads it (below).

A `python` runner's files are wheels, source archives with `extract` (the directory they are unpacked into), and data files with `into` (the directory of the runnable copy they are copied into). A data file is something the runner would otherwise download when it runs. vLLM's `o200k_base.tiktoken`, the tokenizer vocabulary gpt-oss's chat format needs, is pinned this way into `tiktoken/`, and the vLLM adapter points `TIKTOKEN_ENCODINGS_BASE` there. openai_harmony then reads the file and checks its sha256 instead of fetching it from openaipublic (runners plan §6: nothing unpinned is downloaded at run time). vLLM loads harmony only on the first gpt-oss chat request, so a gpt-oss snapshot (`model_type` `gpt_oss`) is refused at start with `runner_incomplete` when the runnable copy lacks the file, for example an install from an older lock.

### Where the files go

| Part | Path | Lifetime |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cache | `/data/runners/<id>/<version>/files/<name>`, and `installed.json`, the install record | Persists: the only part that survives the container |
| Runnable copy | `/opt/runners/<id>/<version>/` in the container's own filesystem. The image creates `/opt/runners` owned by uid 1000. | The container's lifetime |

### Install

| Step | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Start | `local_llm_runner_install { runnerId, acceptLicence }`, admin only. Nothing installs automatically. One install runs at a time. |
| Operator switch | A runner whose adapter has one (LM Studio, `LOCAL_LLM_LMSTUDIO=internal-use`, DS001) is refused with `runner_disabled` while it is off, before anything downloads; the dashboard shows the reason and no Install. Uninstall still works, to free the disk. |
| Licence | A runner whose lock entry sets `requiresAcceptance` is refused with `licence_required` unless `acceptLicence` is true. The acceptance is recorded in the install state and in `installed.json`, with who accepted (the verified caller from the Router-signed invocation, never tool input) and when. The dashboard shows the licence, its source link and the notice before the Install is sent. |
| Download | Each file goes through the downloader's resume, size and free-disk checks and is verified against its sha256 before it is used (`downloadFile`). The whole install first needs free space for the remaining bytes plus 5 %. A Stop, a drain or a network failure leaves the install `paused`; the next Install resumes the partial files. A server that answers a resumed request with 200 and only part of the file (LM Studio's download host does, with no `Content-Range`) makes the downloader discard the partial and start that file again from zero. |
| Record | `installed.json` is written only after every file verified. |
| Runnable copy | Built right after the download (below), so the install also measures the rebuild time. |
| Update | A new lock version is installed beside the old one. The old version's cache and copy are removed only after the new version is in place. |

### Runnable copy

Before the first launch in a container, and at the end of an install, `ensureRunnable` checks the copy's `.ready.json` marker. If the marker names this exact lock entry, the copy is reused, so a process restart in the same container does not rebuild. Otherwise:

1. every cached file is copied into container-local staging (`/opt/runners/.stage-<id>`) and hashed as it is copied; any difference from the lock blocks the rebuild with `cache_changed`. The steps below read only the staged copies, so a file replaced in `/data` after the check cannot reach the runnable copy;
2. the copy's directory is emptied;
3. a `python` runner gets a virtual environment from `/usr/bin/python3` (`uv venv`), and `uv pip install --offline --no-index --find-links <staging> --no-deps --require-hashes --no-cache` installs exactly the locked wheels; source archives are unpacked where the lock says, and data files are copied read-only (0444) into their `into` directory;
4. an `archive` runner's archives are unpacked, dropping one leading directory unless the file says `strip: 0` (LM Studio's llmster tarball has `llmster` and `.bundle/` at its root). File times are not restored (`tar --touch`): on the container's fuse-overlayfs, setting a directory's time fails with `EPERM`;
5. the staging is removed and the marker is written last.

Only one build of a runner's copy runs at a time: a caller that arrives while it is being built (an Install finishing while a Run starts) shares that build. A Run on a runner whose install is in progress is refused with `busy`.

Every step runs in its own process group, so a Stop or a drain ends it. `uv` gets a minimal environment (`UV_OFFLINE`, `UV_PYTHON_DOWNLOADS=never`, no agent secrets). Code changed in the runnable copy lasts only as long as the container, like code baked into the image; `ploinky restart` creates a new container, which rebuilds the copy from the verified cache.

### LM Studio's runnable copy

The lock's `lmstudio` entry is llmster 0.0.25-1 with its bundled CUDA 12 engine, one tarball from `llmster.lmstudio.ai` (1,105,623,572 bytes, sha256 `46778639…`, `strip: 0`), under LM Studio's Terms, marked proprietary. The copy is the unpacked tarball, with no post-install step: llmster runs from it directly, without LM Studio's `install.sh` or `bootstrap`. Its home is `home/` inside the copy. On its first start in a container, llmster moves its engines out of the copy into that home, so the two share one lifetime: a rebuild or an uninstall removes both, and nothing of LM Studio's lives in `/data` except the verified tarball in the cache. The LM Studio SDK the adapter loads through is not part of the copy: it is pinned in the image (`/opt/local-llm/lmstudio-sdk`).

### Uninstall

`local_llm_runner_uninstall { runnerId }` deletes the runner's cache and runnable copy, clears its install state and re-runs runner detection. It is refused while the runner runs a model, and it cancels an install in progress.

### Detection

A runner is installable when it is in the image's lock and this release has an adapter for it; a lock entry without an adapter (a runner a later release will run) is installed only by the CI install check. An installable runner is installed when its cache is complete and its record names the lock entry. Detection reads files only; it never imports Python packages. It runs again after every install and uninstall, so the dashboard and `local_llm_overview` follow without an agent restart. A Run on an installable runner that is not installed is refused with `runner_not_installed`.

### CI install check

The image's publish workflow installs every lock entry inside the published image with `tools/runner_install_check.mjs`, one entry at a time. It checks each pinned distribution's version, imports the modules that load without a GPU, lists the ones that need the driver, and runs `ldd` on every shared object in the runnable copy. A library `ldd` cannot find passes only if the Box GPU grant supplies it (`libcuda.so.1`), if another file in the same environment has that name (wheels load each other's libraries at run time, as torch loads its CUDA libraries), or if the lock entry lists it in `check.optionalLibraries` with the reason the runner never needs it (for example MPI and RDMA libraries for multi-node transports). Any other missing library fails the check, and the report lists all three groups. Every data file (`into`) must also be in the runnable copy with the lock's sha256.

A proprietary entry is never downloaded in CI, because downloading it would accept its terms on behalf of whoever runs CI. The workflow runs the check for it with no network and `--validate-only`, and the check itself also refuses to download any proprietary entry. It reports `downloaded: false` with what the lock pins: the files, their total size, their hosts and the licence fields. The install of such a runner is proven live, on a deployment whose admin accepted its terms.

## Decisions & Questions

### Question #1: Why rebuild the runnable copy instead of running from /data?

Response: `/data` is a workspace bind that survives containers and that other processes with workspace access can write. Rebuilding into the container's own filesystem from a cache that is re-verified against the image's lock means that code changed on disk never outlives the container, the same guarantee code baked into the image has. The check and the build use the same bytes: each file is hashed while it is copied into container-local staging, and the build reads only that copy, so a writer that swaps a cached file after the check gains nothing.

### Question #2: Why `--no-deps` with the full closure?

Response: The lock already lists the resolved closure for this image's Python, so the install needs no resolver: every wheel is named with its hash, and nothing else can be installed.

# Advanced Language Agent

[Advanced Language Agent](docs/index.html) (ALA) is a command-line application for language and documentation tasks. It executes general requests through AchillesAgentLib and delegates bounded work to an installed coding agent. ALA mounts exactly the directories the caller supplies through `--cwd` and `--folder`; it does not discover, create, mount or overlay task skills. ALA writes the result to standard output or a file.

## Install

ALA requires Node.js 20 or newer, npm, and Git. Coding-agent execution additionally requires Linux with Bubblewrap (`bwrap`); ALA fails closed instead of starting Codex, OpenCode, or Pi without it. Coding-agent CLIs remain installed once in their normal system or user locations: ALA never reinstalls or copies them. It resolves each launcher to its existing runtime prefix, mounts that prefix read-only, and prefers its matching executable path inside the sandbox. Prefixes below the mounted working directory use a private runtime path so the workspace mount cannot hide the installed executable; other prefixes retain their existing paths. An external target of `/etc/resolv.conf` is mounted read-only when systemd-resolved stores it under `/run`. Codex and OpenCode also require Bubblewrap to mount a private procfs; ALA never substitutes the caller's `/proc`. It first uses a private user namespace. In a capability-bounded nested container where that extra user namespace cannot mount procfs, ALA may use the outer sandbox capability to construct the PID namespace and private procfs, then drops all capabilities before starting the coding agent. Codex is told not to construct a second native sandbox: its `danger-full-access` setting is scoped inside ALA's Bubblewrap boundary, where only the mounted directories and controlled home remain writable. Direct MainAgent execution remains available without a coding agent. From the repository root, run:

```sh
npm install
```

This installs AchillesAgentLib from the Git dependency in `package.json`.

Add the project's `bin` directory to `PATH`. Put this line in `~/.bashrc` when the repository is located at `$HOME/Desktop/work/AdvancedLanguageAgent`:

```sh
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/Desktop/work/AdvancedLanguageAgent/bin"
```

Reload the shell configuration and verify the installation:

```sh
source ~/.bashrc
ala --version
ala --help
```

## Configure

ALA can use [Soul Gateway](docs/wiki.html#definition-soul-gateway) or your own AchillesAgentLib-compatible model configuration.

To use Soul Gateway, create a `.env` file in the directory where you run ALA or in one of its parent directories:

```dotenv
SOUL_GATEWAY_BASE_URL=https://your-soul-gateway.example
SOUL_GATEWAY_API_KEY=your-api-key
```

AchillesAgentLib loads the first `.env` file it finds while walking upward from the current working directory. With the bundled model configuration, ALA uses the Soul Gateway `plan` model by default.

input.description: Audit Ploinky GPU plumbing on arm64
input.prompt:
We are planning a new Ploinky agent `dgx-local-agent` that runs local LLMs on an NVIDIA DGX Spark (this machine: aarch64, NVIDIA GB10 Grace Blackwell, compute capability 12.1 / sm_121, 128 GB unified CPU/GPU memory, driver 580.159.03, CUDA 13.0, DGX OS / Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.17). Ploinky runs every agent as a nested rootless podman container inside a "Box" container (currently `ploinky-box-work-287e15733c26`, image docker.io/assistos/ploinky-box:latest). Your job: a READ-ONLY audit of what in Ploinky core blocks or constrains GPU agents on this arm64 host, and what minimal changes would fix it. Do not modify any files and do not restart/stop any containers.

Known so far:
- `ploinky gpu status` (run `/home/research/work/ploinky/bin/ploinky gpu status` from /home/research/work) says: "Host GPU: unavailable (NVIDIA driver library libcuda.so.1 is not in the ldconfig cache)". Cause: `parseLdconfigCache` in /home/research/work/ploinky/ploinky-box/gpuGrant.mjs (~line 232) only accepts ldconfig entries whose flags include `x86-64`; on this host they are `libc6,AArch64`.
- Host has /etc/cdi/nvidia.yaml (NVIDIA Container Toolkit 1.19.1) and /dev/nvidia0, /dev/nvidiactl, /dev/nvidia-uvm, /dev/nvidia-uvm-tools, /dev/nvidia-modeset, /dev/nvidia-caps.
- nvidia-smi on GB10 reports memory.total/used/free as `[N/A]`.

Please investigate and report:
1. Every x86-64 / discrete-GPU assumption in /home/research/work/ploinky/ploinky-box/gpuGrant.mjs and ploinky-box/lib/gpuGrantMarker.mjs (and anything they call): ldconfig parsing, required/optional library list, device node list, bind paths (/usr/local/nvidia/lib64, /usr/local/nvidia/bin), CDI spec generation (`ploinky.local/gpu=all`), fingerprinting, driver version checks. Compare Ploinky's required library list against what the host's /etc/cdi/nvidia.yaml lists for this GB10 (read that file) — which libraries/devices/hooks does NVIDIA's own CDI spec include that Ploinky would omit and that CUDA 13 / vLLM / llama.cpp / NCCL on GB10 likely need (e.g. libnvidia-gpucomp, libnvidia-nvvm, libcudadebugger, firmware, /dev/nvidia-caps, IMEX, etc.)? Also check whether the tests under /home/research/work/ploinky/tests cover gpuGrant parsing and would need arm64 fixtures.
2. How the manifest field `containerSecurity` is applied to nested agent containers: find where `gpu`, `shmSize`, `privileged` and any other supported keys (ulimits? memlock? ipc? pids?) are translated into podman args. List every supported key and its validation. Specifically: can an agent get `--ipc host`, `--ulimit memlock=-1`, `--ulimit stack=67108864`, a large /dev/shm (e.g. 16g+), and access to the CUDA device without privileged? What's the Box's own resource/cgroup situation (memory limits? pids limits?) — check `podman inspect ploinky-box-work-287e15733c26` for Memory, PidsLimit, ShmSize, Devices, security opts (read-only inspect is OK).
3. Is the Box image / ploinky-node image multi-arch (they run here on aarch64, so presumably yes)? Look at /home/research/work/.ploinky/repos/container-image-builds/images/ploinky-box and ploinky-node and the repo's CI workflows (.github) to see how multi-arch builds are done (buildx platforms?), so a new arm64+CUDA agent image could follow the same publishing pattern. Report the exact workflow file(s) and platform flags.
4. Anything in Ploinky docs/proposals about GPU (search for "D14", "gpu", "CDI" in /home/research/work/ploinky/docs, /home/research/work/ploinky/proposals, README.md, CLAUDE.md) that documents design intent, and whether multiple agents can hold the GPU grant simultaneously (e.g. `local-llms/local-llm` and a new `dgx-local/dgx-local-agent`).
5. The nested network model: can an agent container reach the host's high-speed ConnectX-7 interfaces (for future multi-Spark), or host networking at all? Just summarize what's supported (host network option?) — brief.

Deliver: a concise but concrete report with file:line references, a table of blockers (severity: hard-blocker / degrades / cosmetic), and a proposed minimal patch list for Ploinky core (describe the diff precisely, e.g. "accept `AArch64` flag when process.arch==='arm64'", add library X to optional list, etc.). Keep it under ~1200 words.

input.prompt:

On GB10, `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total,memory.used,memory.free` returns `[N/A]` (so local-llm's src/controller/hardware.mjs `readGpu` yields NaN), and there is no separate VRAM: "CPU offload" does not add capacity. The existing local-llm image is linux/amd64 only, CUDA 12.8, ik_llama.cpp built for sm_86/sm_89. READ-ONLY: do not modify any files.

1. Read every module under /home/research/work/.ploinky/repos/local-llms/local-llm/src (controller/*, runners/*, main.mjs, controlSocket.mjs, chatResponder.mjs, testPrompt.mjs, drainBudget.mjs, errors.mjs), tools/*, catalog/models.json + schema.json, mcp-config.json, and skim the IDE-plugins and tests. Pay special attention to: admission.mjs (VRAM vs RAM split, cpuOffloadGb, 94% usable, 90% cap, GPU margin/RAM margin, memory guard), hardware.mjs, the runner adapter contract in runners/index.mjs + params.mjs (what fields an adapter must provide — list them precisely, since new adapters like TensorRT-LLM/SGLang/llama.cpp-sm121 would implement it), vllm.mjs (flags it passes: --enforce-eager? --gpu-memory-utilization? cpu offload? max-model-len? tool/reasoning parsers?), llamaServer.mjs (flags: -fa, --no-mmap?, -ngl, --n-cpu-moe, --jinja?, -np, cache types), deployments.mjs (the "one deployment at a time" constraint — how deeply is it baked in? what would it take to run 2–3 concurrent deployments, e.g. a small fast model + a big coder model, which the 128 GB machine can afford?), downloader.mjs/weightStores.mjs (formats gguf/ollama/hf/exl3; could NVFP4/MXFP4 HF snapshots and TensorRT-LLM checkpoints fit?), runnerLock.mjs/runnerInstaller.mjs (lock schema, allowed hosts, python wheel installs via uv — would aarch64 wheels for vLLM cu130 fit this model or is a container-image approach better?), chatResponder.mjs (8192 max_tokens clamp, 570s timeout, field allowlist — does it pass through tools/tool_choice/stream/reasoning fields?).
2. Read the image build: /home/research/work/.ploinky/repos/container-image-builds/images/local-llm (Dockerfile, runners.lock.json, any scripts) and the publish workflow in /home/research/work/.ploinky/repos/container-image-builds/.github/workflows (find the local-llm one). List every arch/CUDA-version assumption (base image, CUDA 12.8, sm_86/89, amd64-only, uv python version, Ollama binary arch, llama.cpp build flags).
3. Assess: forking local-llm vs extracting a shared core library vs adding a "dgx" hardware profile inside local-llm itself. Which modules would be duplicated in a fork, and roughly how many lines? Are there clean seams (dependency injection points, adapter registry, hardware snapshot interface) that make a "hardware profile" plug-in feasible?

Run the existing test suite to see its baseline on this machine: from /home/research/work/.ploinky/repos/local-llms run `node --test 'local-llm/tests/*.test.mjs' 2>&1 | tail -30` (Node 24 is at /usr/bin/node; if the Node version here lacks something, just report). Report pass/fail counts and any failures that look arch-related.

Based on the search results, here's information about llama.cpp router mode and the features you're asking about:

## Router Mode Overview

llama.cpp server now ships with router mode, which lets you dynamically load, unload, and switch between multiple models without restarting.

## Using --models-dir

You can point the router to a local directory containing your GGUF files using --models-dir. All model instances inherit settings from the router: llama-server --models-dir ./models -c 8192 -ngl 99 · All loaded models will use 8192 context and full GPU offload.

## Loading and Unloading on Demand

The router discovers multiple GGUF models and loads or unloads them on demand. Start llama-server without a -m flag and it becomes a router: a lightweight proxy that owns the port, discovers the GGUF files available to it, and spawns each requested model as its own child process.

## Model Presets

With --models-preset, you can register multiple models in one preset file, expose them behind one stable OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and route requests using the "model" field in /v1/chat/completions.

## Important Considerations

Even though multiple models are defined in models.ini, only one is resident in VRAM per worker at any given moment. Switching means a full unload-and-reload cycle.

content.text:
The three analyses are still running: Ploinky's arm64 GPU plumbing, how other agents consume local models, and what in `local-llm` can be reused. I'll put the plan together once they finish.

What I've confirmed so far on this machine:

- **The existing `local-llm` agent can't run here.**
  - Its image is amd64-only, built for CUDA 12.8 on older GPUs.
  - Explorer enabled it anyway. The Box spent 10 minutes pulling 4.6 GB, then failed with `Exec format error`.
- **Ploinky's GPU access check only works on x86.** It only looks for x86-64 driver libraries, so `ploinky gpu status` reports "Host GPU: unavailable" even though the GB10 works fine. No agent can get the GPU here until that's fixed in Ploinky itself.
- **GB10 reports no memory numbers.** `nvidia-smi` returns `[N/A]` for memory, and `local-llm`'s memory checks assume a separate GPU memory pool. With 128 GB shared between CPU and GPU, the whole "does this model fit?" check has to be redesigned.
- **Disk is tighter than expected.** This is the 1 TB model with only 132 GB free, which is room for roughly one or two large models (gpt-oss-120b alone is about 60 GB). The agent will need a disk budget and a way to evict old weights.
- **This is a single Spark.** All four high-speed network ports are down, so multi-machine setups are out of scope for a first version.
- **vLLM is viable on arm64.** vLLM 0.30.0 has an arm64 package on PyPI built for CUDA 13, and its official images come in arm64 builds too. The existing approach of installing vLLM on demand from a pinned lock file should carry over.

<result>I found one hard blocker for a CUDA agent on this host: the ldconfig architecture filter. The rest of the GPU path is not arch-specific. The other items limit or slow a vLLM/llama.cpp agent without stopping it, apart from multi-Spark networking, which the Box design rules out. This was read-only: no files changed and no containers restarted. The only things I ran were the three GPU/runtime unit test files (70 pass), and read-only commands inside the Box through `podman exec`.

## 1. GPU grant code (`ploinky-box/gpuGrant.mjs`)

- **`:232-243` `parseLdconfigCache`**: line 239 only accepts entries flagged `x86-64`. On this host every entry is `libc6,AArch64` (zero x86-64 entries out of 1418), so discovery fails. The version parser (`:245`) already handles "Kernel Module for aarch64 580.159.03".
- **What happens once the parser is fixed:** discovery should pass on this host.
  - The 3 device nodes (`:49`) exist and are `rw-rw-rw-`.
  - The required libraries (`:53-57`) resolve to `/usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/*.so.580.159.03`.
  - The optional `libnvidia-nvvm.so.4` and `libnvidia-gpucomp.so.580.159.03` (`:58`, `:337`) are in the ldconfig cache.
  - `/usr/bin/nvidia-smi` is there.
  - The `/usr/local/nvidia/{lib64,bin}` paths (`constants.mjs:41-46`) are arch-neutral.
- **CDI spec (`:397-418`)** has no hooks and no env: device nodes plus read-only binds only. So there is no `libcuda.so` symlink, no ld-cache update and no `enable-cuda-compat`.
- **Fingerprint (`:464-478`) and observation regex (`:760`, `:776`)** have no arch assumptions.
- **`gpuGrantMarker.mjs`** is arch-neutral.

**Compared with NVIDIA's `/etc/cdi/nvidia.yaml`, Ploinky leaves out:**
- **Needed for compute, and missing:**
  - `libnvidia-nvvm70.so.4`: `libcuda` loads it by name (seen in its strings), but ldconfig lists only `libcuda.so.1`, not the unversioned `libcuda.so`. Its real file is named `.so.4`, so the `versionedName` check (`:323`) would reject it as written.
  - The unversioned `libcuda.so` symlink: Triton, which vLLM uses, links against `-lcuda`.
  - The forward-compat hook: without it the agent image's CUDA must be 13.0 or lower (driver 580).
- **Useful for profiling only:** `/dev/nvidia-uvm-tools` (CUPTI/Nsight).
- **Not needed for CUDA inference:** `/dev/nvidia-modeset`, `/dev/dri/*`, `libcudadebugger`, `libnvidia-cfg`/`opencl`/`encode`/`nvcuvid`, the GL/EGL/Vulkan libraries, the GSP firmware, the persistenced socket and the MPS binaries.
- **`/dev/nvidia-caps` and IMEX:** NVIDIA's own spec omits them too. `nvidia-cap1` is root-only, and no IMEX channels exist. Not needed.
- **`nvidia-smi` memory `[N/A]`:** Ploinky core never reads it (`cli/sandbox/docker/hardwareDetection.js:89` runs only `nvidia-smi -L`). Only the local-llm agent parses it (`src/controller/hardware.mjs:29`).

**Tests:** `tests/unit/ploinkyBoxGpuGrant.test.mjs:61-62`, `:101`, `:114` and `:296` use x86-only fixtures (`/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu`, `(libc6,x86-64)`). They pass here only because the parser is hard-coded. An arch-aware parser that defaults to `process.arch` would break them on arm64 unless the arch is injected. They need arm64 fixtures.

## 2. `containerSecurity` and the runtime policy

- **Supported keys** (`cli/sandbox/runtimeCapabilities.js:26`, validated at `:218-259`):
  - `gpu` (boolean)
  - `nestedPodman` (boolean)
  - `privileged` (boolean; refused inside a Box, `:500`)
  - `shmSize` (`^[1-9]\d{0,5}[mg]$`, capped at 16g, `:29-30`)
- **Resource knobs** go through `llmRuntime.runtimePolicy`. It applies to any agent and does not need `enabled` (`:415`, `agentServiceManager.js:1785`). Keys: `platform`, `resources{memory,cpus,pidsLimit,shmSize,ulimits.memlock{soft,hard}}`, `devices`, `securityOpt`, `ipc`, `gpus` (`containerRuntimePolicy.js:67-106`, `:168-204`; output at `:254-306`).

| Requirement | Possible? |
|---|---|
| GPU device without privileged | Yes. `gpu:true` gets exactly `--device ploinky.local/gpu=all` (`:434-452`). No extra `/dev/dri` is allowed alongside it (`:164`). |
| `--ipc host` | No. Refused inside a Box (`:507`). The agent always gets `--ipc private` (`containerRuntimePolicy.js:299`). |
| `--ulimit memlock=-1` | Yes, via `resources.ulimits.memlock:{soft:-1,hard:-1}`. The Box's hard memlock limit is unlimited. |
| `--ulimit stack=67108864` | No key for it. The agent can raise its own soft limit (`ulimit -s`), since the Box's hard stack limit is unlimited. |
| `/dev/shm` of 16g or more | Up to exactly 16g. |

**Box container (read-only inspect):**
- Memory: unlimited. PidsLimit: **2048** (podman's default; the create command at `lifecycle/container.mjs:155-200` passes no `--pids-limit`). Currently 716 used, peak 877.
- ShmSize 64 MB (the Box's own; agents get their own `/dev/shm`). No devices (no grant yet). SecurityOpt: `label=disable`, `unmask=all`, nested seccomp. Not privileged.
- The Box's `/etc/containers/containers.conf` sets `cgroups="disabled"`. So `memory`, `pidsLimit` and `cpus` are not enforced on nested agents (running agents show Pids=0, Mem=0), and all agents share the Box's 2048-pid cap.

## 3. Multi-arch images

- **ploinky-box** (`.github/workflows/publish-ploinky-box-image.yml:45-58`, `:158`, `:288`) and **ploinky-node** (`publish-ploinky-node-image.yml`) both work the same way:
  - a matrix builds amd64 on `ubuntu-24.04` and arm64 on `ubuntu-24.04-arm`, natively (no QEMU);
  - each job runs `docker/build-push-action` with `platforms: ${{ matrix.platform }}` and `push-by-digest=true`;
  - a proof job runs per arch;
  - an `assemble` job runs `docker buildx imagetools create` from the two proven digests.
- The live `ploinky-box:latest` is an OCI index with amd64 and arm64 entries.
- **local-llm is amd64-only** (`publish-local-llm-image.yml:3-5`, `:68`; pinned x86 CUDA builds). It cannot run on this host.
- For a new arm64 CUDA image, copy the ploinky-node pattern, using a single arm64 matrix entry or both. The hosted arm runners have no GPU, so the proof step can only use `ldd` with `libcuda` excluded, as local-llm does (`:109-120`).

## 4. Design intent (D14)

- D14 is documented in `README.md:652-753`, `CLAUDE.md` invariant 4, `docs/specs/DS005…:116-119` and `DS014…:57,69`. `proposals/` has nothing on GPU.
- **Several agents can hold the GPU at the same time.** The wiring is a set of up to 64 agents (`gpuGrant.mjs:146`, `:80`), and each one gets the same `ploinky.local/gpu=all` device. There is no exclusivity or memory accounting, so `local-llms/local-llm` and `dgx-local/dgx-local-agent` can both be named. They will compete for the 128 GB unified pool and have to coordinate between themselves.

## 5. Networking

- `network.mode:"host"` (`agentServiceManager.js:837`) gives the agent the **Box's** network namespace, not the physical host's.
- The Box uses `pasta:--ipv4-only` and sees only a copy of `wlP9s9`: no ConnectX-7 interfaces and no `/dev/infiniband`.
- Outbound TCP follows the host's routing through pasta. Inbound connections from other Sparks are impossible by invariant 3 (only two publications allowed).
- So NCCL/RoCE across several Sparks is blocked by design, not by a bug.

## Blockers

| # | Item | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| B1 | ldconfig parser accepts only `x86-64` (`gpuGrant.mjs:239`) | hard-blocker |
| B2 | local-llm image is amd64-only | hard-blocker (for reusing it) |
| B3 | Multi-Spark: no host network, RDMA or inbound access (invariant 3) | hard-blocker (future, by design) |

The Ploinky GPU audit is back, and it's good news: **one small parser fix in Ploinky core unblocks GPU access on this machine**. The rest of the GPU path doesn't depend on the CPU architecture, and several agents can hold the GPU at the same time.

It also found constraints the design has to live with:
- **Shared memory is capped at 16 GB.** Agents can't get `--ipc host`, and `/dev/shm` stops at `16g`.
- **Process limit.** All agents share the Box's 2,048-process cap.
- **No per-agent memory limits.** Nested memory and CPU limits aren't enforced, so the new agent has to police its own memory use.
- **CUDA version ceiling.** The image's CUDA must be 13.0 or lower, because there's no forward-compatibility hook.
- **No multi-Spark.** Linking several Sparks is blocked by design: the Box can't see the high-speed network interfaces.

Still waiting on the other two analyses (model consumers, and what in `local-llm` can be reused).

<result>## local-llm reuse audit for a DGX Spark agent (GB10, aarch64, UMA)

**Most important finding:** local-llm on this machine doesn't just fail, it approves everything. `readGpu` (`src/controller/hardware.mjs:63-65`) turns `[N/A]` into NaN, and every comparison with NaN in `admission.mjs` is false. I ran `admit()` against a live GB10 snapshot: every seed model returned `ok`, and so did a made-up 500 GiB dense GGUF and a 300 GiB vLLM snapshot. vLLM then fails at launch, because `gpuMemoryUtilization` comes out as NaN and `vllm.mjs:116` throws `invalid_launch`. All GPU checks are silently off.

Nothing was modified. The only file I wrote was a small admission probe in the scratchpad.

### 1. Module classification

A = reuse as-is, B = reuse with changes, C = replace.

| Module | Purpose | Class and what changes |
|---|---|---|
| `main.mjs`, `controlSocket.mjs`, `errors.mjs`, `drainBudget.mjs` | Main process, private control socket with token, drain timing | A |
| `testPrompt.mjs` | Admin smoke chat over loopback | A. Only the `GATEWAY_MODEL` name changes (`:19`, `deployments.mjs:363`) |
| `chatResponder.mjs` | `/v1/chat/completions` proxy | B (see §1d) |
| `controller/commandQueue.mjs` | Serialized mutations | A |
| `controller/stateStore.mjs` | Atomic state writes and restart recovery | A for one deployment, B for several (`deployment: null` at `:21`, `reconcileAfterRestart` `:100-119`) |
| `controller/catalog.mjs` + `schema.json` | Catalog validation | B. GGUF is one file only (`:73-77`), so split GGUFs (`-0000N-of-M`, common for 60–120 GB models) can't be expressed. Snapshots are top-level files only (`:102`) |
| `controller/downloader.mjs`, `weightStores.mjs`, `ollamaStore.mjs` | Resumable, sha256-pinned downloads | A. Add a multi-file GGUF store by reusing the snapshot code |
| `controller/runnerProcess.mjs` | Process group, log buffer, report parser | A (the `CUDA0` regexes still match on GB10) |
| `controller/hardware.mjs` | Hardware snapshot | C for `readGpu`/`readSnapshot`. `physicalCoreCount` is A (returns 20 here). `defaultThreads` is B: 18 threads includes the A725 efficiency cores |
| `controller/admission.mjs` | Fit decisions | C (§1a) |
| `controller/runnerLock.mjs` | Runner lock schema | B. `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (`:42-51`) has no `pypi.nvidia.com` or `wheels.vllm.ai`. Files have no platform field (`:106-143`), so one lock = one architecture |
| `controller/runnerInstaller.mjs` | Offline `uv` venv build | B. Python is fixed to `/usr/bin/python3` 3.13 (`:28`, `:284`, `UV_PYTHON_DOWNLOADS=never`); TensorRT-LLM has historically shipped cp310/cp312 wheels only |
| `controller/deployments.mjs` | The controller | B. Nothing arch-specific, but one deployment is assumed throughout (§1c) |
| `runners/index.mjs`, `params.mjs` | Adapter registry, param validation | A |
| `runners/llamaServer.mjs`, `llamaCpp.mjs` | llama-server family | B: new sm_121 binary, and `admit` is hard-wired (`llamaServer.mjs:236`) |
| `runners/ikLlamaCpp.mjs` | ik fork | C. Its hybrid CPU/GPU MoE advantage means nothing on UMA; drop it |
| `runners/ollama.mjs` | Ollama | B: arm64 binary; `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=1` (`:109`); `admitOllama` is C |
| `runners/vllm.mjs` | vLLM | B (§1b) |
| `runners/tabbyApi.mjs` | ExLlamaV3 | C: cu128 x86 wheels, sm_121 support unknown |
| `runners/lmStudio.mjs`, `lmStudioLoad.mjs` | LM Studio | C: `ENGINE_DIR` is the x86_64 CUDA 12 engine (`:37`), and it's proprietary |
| `tools/local_llm_tool.mjs`, `runner_install_check.mjs` | MCP tool dispatch, CI install check | A (B once tools take a deployment id) |
| `catalog/models.json` | Seed models | C. Its values are tuned for a 6 GB card (e.g. `nCpuMoe: 17`). It is swappable through `LOCAL_LLM_CATALOG_FILE` (`deployments.mjs:70`) |
| `mcp-config.json` | 12 admin tools | A, or B for multi-deployment |
| IDE plugins (1,599 lines of JS) | Dashboard | B. The GPU card and estimate meter read `gpu.totalBytes/usedBytes` (`local-llm-dashboard-view.js:63-71, 350-357`), which are NaN here |

**1a. `admission.mjs` is built on a separate VRAM pool and RAM pool.**
- **llama-server estimate:** weights are split into `gpuWeights`/`cpuWeights` by `nCpuMoe`. The GPU part is checked against `gpu.totalBytes*0.97` and `gpu.freeBytes-256 MiB` (`:132, :140`); the RAM part separately against `availableBytes-1 GiB` (`:144`). On UMA those two checks double-count one pool.
- **vLLM:** `VLLM_USABLE_SHARE 0.94`, `VLLM_MAX_UTILIZATION 0.9` and the 768 MiB overhead (`:200-203`) were measured on an RTX 3060. The GPU share it passes vLLM is computed from free VRAM (`fromFree`, `:231`, NaN here).
- **vLLM `cpuOffloadGb`:** its RAM estimate is 1.81× the offload + 3 GiB, ×1.15 (`:214-218`). On UMA, offload adds no capacity and would consume the same pool twice.
- **Memory guard:** it only runs when admission sets `ramFloorBytes`, i.e. vLLM with offload (`deployments.mjs:530-560`). With no swap on this machine, it should run for every deployment.

**1b. `vllm.mjs` flags** (`:121-135`):
- Always passed: `--model`, `--served-model-name`, `--host 127.0.0.1`, `--port`, `--max-model-len` (default 4096, max 131072), `--gpu-memory-utilization`, `--max-num-seqs` (default 1), `--dtype`.
- Conditional: `--enforce-eager` (on by default), `--quantization`, `--kv-cache-dtype`, `--cpu-offload-gb`.
- Not passed at all: `--enable-auto-tool-choice`, `--tool-call-parser`, `--reasoning-parser`, `--max-num-batched-tokens`, `--trust-remote-code`. So `tools` with `tool_choice: auto` will fail on vLLM.
- Environment: FlashInfer sampler is off because the image has no CUDA toolkit. Compile caches are container-local (`:189`), so CUDA graphs and torch.compile are rebuilt on every container start.

**llama-server flags** (`llamaServer.mjs:161-201`): `-m`, `--host`, `--port`, `--api-key`, `--no-webui -lv 4`, `--alias`, `--ctx-size` (16k), `--n-gpu-layers` 99, `--n-cpu-moe` only if >0, `--flash-attn` auto, `--cache-type-k/v` (f16 default; q8_0 and q4_0 also allowed), `--threads`, `-np` 1, `--kv-unified` when np>1, batch 2048 / ubatch 512, `--load-mode` (mmap stays on unless `noMmap` is set), `--chat-template-kwargs`, and `--jinja` only when the model sets `requiresJinja`.

**1c. "One deployment at a time" is built in deeply, but only in the controller, state and UI, not in the adapters.** Running 2–3 concurrent deployments would take:
- **State and controller:** the single `state.deployment` (31 references), plus the single `job`, `runner`, `runnerLogStart`, `lastCompletion` and `memoryStop` (`deployments.mjs:110-129`), become per-deployment maps. The busy/replace check (`:813-820`), `inUse` and drain handle several.
- **Ports and scratch dirs:** ports are fixed per runner (`ports[runnerId]`, `:617`, `index.mjs:33`), so two llama.cpp instances collide; ports must be allocated per deployment. vLLM and TabbyAPI use fixed `/dev/shm` directories (`vllm.mjs:29`, `tabbyApi.mjs:29`) that also collide.
- **Routing:** `chatTarget()` must take a model id. `buildRunnerRequest` must stop overwriting `model` (`chatResponder.mjs:100`). The manifest needs an `endpoints.models` command; AgentServer supports this (`resolveOpenAiModelsKind`), whereas the fallback only lists `default`. Whether Soul Gateway exposes several ids per agent still needs checking.
- **Admission:** it has to check the sum of all running deployments' estimates against the shared pool.
- **Surface:** the tools, the per-deployment log, and the dashboard's single deployment card.
- **Size:** roughly 1.5–2.5k changed lines, most of them in `deployments.mjs` and the dashboard.

**1d. `chatResponder.mjs`.**
- **Passed through** (`:12-16`): `tools`, `tool_choice`, `stream`, `stream_options`, `response_format`, `reasoning_effort`, `chat_template_kwargs`, `logprobs`, `top_logprobs`.
- **Dropped:** `parallel_tool_calls`, the `reasoning` object, `top_k`, `min_p`, `repetition_penalty`, `logit_bias`, `user`, and vLLM extras.
- **Limits:** `MAX_COMPLETION_TOKENS` 8192 and `RUNNER_TIMEOUT_MS` 570 s are hard-coded (`:76-77`). A big dense model at about 5 tok/s cannot produce 8192 tokens within 570 s.

**1e. Weight formats.**
- NVFP4 (ModelOpt) and MXFP4 Hugging Face snapshots fit the `hf` format when their files are top-level `.safetensors`/`.json`; the `quantization` pattern accepts `modelopt_fp4` and `mxfp4`.
- TensorRT-LLM checkpoints fit the same way through its PyTorch backend, which reads HF checkpoints. Prebuilt `.engine` files don't fit the snapshot file pattern, and since engines are specific to the GPU they should be built locally anyway.
- Split GGUFs need a new source type.

**1f. Runner adapter contract.** This is what a TensorRT-LLM, SGLang or llama.cpp-sm121 adapter would implement.
- **Required fields and functions:**

  - `endpoints.chatCompletions` only sets `responderKind` (70-82):

- **Soul Gateway turns agents into models.**

  - It then GETs `/<routeKey>/v1/models` through the Router (`runtime/backends/builtin/ploinky-agent-openai.backend.mjs:214-257`) and syncs with `disableMissing:true` (`reconcile-agents.mjs:540-557`). An empty list never disables anything (`runtime/providers/auto-provisioner.mjs:534-544`).
  - Model key = `${repo}/${agent}/${modelId}`, where `modelId = row.modelId || row.providerModelId || row.id` (backend 405-420).
- **Where `/default` comes from.** AgentServer's `/v1/models` (`PL/Agent/server/AgentServer.mjs:843-870`) runs `endpoints.models.command` if one is declared. Otherwise it returns a fallback (810-841): a single row with `id:'default'` and `displayName` set to the agent name. The row also carries `supportsTools:true`, `supportsVision:false`, and tags from `capabilities.tags`, or `['generic-agent']` when none are declared (813).
  - If model sync fails, Soul Gateway also writes a `<repo>/<agent>/default` placeholder (`reconcile-agents.mjs:108-151`).
- **Multiple models per agent: yes, already supported.**
  - Declare `endpoints.models.command` returning `{object:'list', data:[{id:'coder',…},{id:'fast'},{id:'big'}]}`. That yields `dgx-local/dgx-local-agent/coder` and so on.
  - Soul Gateway sends `model: providerModelId` (e.g. `"coder"`) in the chat body (backend 146, 289-293), so the chat handler must dispatch on `request.model`. The existing local-llm ignores it: it overwrites `body.model` at `LL/src/chatResponder.mjs:100`.

## 2. Protocols

The chain is: client → Soul Gateway ingress → `ploinky-agent-openai` backend → Router, which only delegates the exact paths `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/models` (`PL/cli/server/agentOpenAiDelegation.js:44-57, 258-312`) → AgentServer (1405) → the command handler. The handler receives `{endpoint:'openai.chat.completions', request, metadata}` on stdin (693-700).

| Feature | Status on this path |
|---|---|
| Streaming (SSE) | **Yes.** Soul Gateway requests `stream:true` whenever the model row says it supports streaming, whatever the client asked (backend 169-178, 289-293). AgentServer pipes handler stdout raw (730-807) and the Router pipes the response back (`routerHandlers.js:208-228`). The default `llm` responder only fakes SSE with a single chunk (`AgentServer.mjs:427-445`). |
| `tools`, `tool_choice`, `tool_calls` | **Yes.** Forwarded at backend 157-160; parsed for streaming (601-613) and non-streaming (665-680) responses. |
| Other request fields | Only `max_tokens`, `temperature`, `top_p`, `stop`, `response_format` and the provider's `settings.extra_body` are forwarded (backend 144-167). **Dropped:** `reasoning_effort`, `chat_template_kwargs`, `seed`, penalties, `n`, `logprobs`, `parallel_tool_calls`, `stream_options`, `max_completion_tokens`. |
| `reasoning_content` | **Not supported.** It is ignored at backend 596-613, and Soul Gateway's internal stream has no reasoning event (`runtime/kernel/canonical-stream.mjs:1-45`). The agent backend also sends no keep-alive signal during reasoning, so a long think counts as silence for the timeouts (`runtime/execution/timeout-middleware.mjs:15-40, 143-157`). |
| Large contexts | Body limits are not the problem: 5 MiB in Soul Gateway (`BODY_LIMIT_BYTES`, `config/env.mjs:136`) and 10 MiB in the Router (`routerHandlers.js:22`). No context-window check exists. The real limit is time: the default request deadline is 120 s (`config/env.mjs:54-57`) and stream idle is 300 s. Token usage is read from any chunk (backend ~617-626). |

- **Anthropic `/v1/messages`:** only at the gateway. Soul Gateway accepts `/v1/messages` and `/v1/responses` (`public-api/register-routes.mjs:31-36`) and converts them into OpenAI chat calls to the agent. AgentServer serves only `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/models` (44-45), and the Router delegates only those two paths.
- **Other endpoint kinds:** a manifest can declare only `chatCompletions`, `models` and `agent-card` (`PL/docs/specs/DS005-agent-manifest-and-registry.md:143-152`).
  - Soul Gateway has `/v1/embeddings`, but it needs a backend with `embed()` (only `openai-api.backend.mjs` has one) and a model tagged `embeddings` (`public-api/embeddings-route.mjs:20, 204-211`).
  - There is no rerank or legacy completions path to agents.

## 3. Tiering

- **AchillesAgentLib just points at gateway tiers.** `LLMConfig.json` `defaults` maps each intent to a Soul Gateway tier: `fast→soul_gateway/fast`, `code/coding→soul_gateway/code`, `plan/thinking/vision→soul_gateway/plan`, `deep/research/long-context→soul_gateway/deep`, plus `write` and `ultra`.
  - Resolution order (`utils/LLMClient.mjs:172-217`): explicit model through the defaults map → `modelConfig[tag]` → tag scoring over discovered models (80-111) → `plan`.
  - Gateway models appear as `soul_gateway/<key>` (`providers/modelsConfigLoader.mjs:532-610`).
  - Per-process override: `LLM_MODELS_CONFIG_PATH` (620-623). The AdvancedLanguageAgent CLI adds `--model`, `ALA_MODEL`, `--tag` and `--model-config`.
- **The tiers themselves live in Soul Gateway.** `fast, code, plan, write, deep, ultra, web-assist` are cascades seeded once from free OpenRouter models (`bootstrap/free-model-catalog.mjs:167-240`; `LLM_DEFAULT_TIERS` at `manifest.json:84`).
- **How tags interact with tiers.**
  - Agent tags are kept as-is; the tag classifier is skipped for discovered agents (`runtime/policy/model-metadata-classifier.mjs:614-615, 643`).
  - Every predefined tag (49-78) except the public tier names (`bootstrap/reconcile-tag-tiers.mjs:10-13`) is an automatic tier. Agent models join it, and for agent providers the tier is created if missing (`reconcile-tag-tiers.mjs:261-330`; `auto-provisioner.mjs:701-709`).
  - `generic-agent` is one of these tags, so every agent without `capabilities.tags` lands in the `generic-agent` cascade.
  - `local-llm` is not a predefined tag. local-llm therefore joins no tier and is reachable only by its explicit id.
- **Mapping `fast` or `code` to a local model: yes, but it is manual.** Public tiers are never filled from tags. An admin edits the tier's children in the Soul Gateway dashboard (Explorer Settings → "Soul Gateway") or via the `/management/tiers` API (`management/tiers-route.mjs:1-17`; `dashboard/js/app.mjs:2636-2808`). This applies to the whole workspace; `LLMConfig.json` `defaults` is the per-client alternative.

## 4. Explorer integration

- **local-llm is enabled by default.** `EXP/manifest.json:11-29` lists `"local-llms/local-llm no-wait"` (28) and `"proxies/soul-gateway no-wait"` (24), and `repos.local-llms` clones the repo (30-35).
- **How plugins are loaded.** The `collect_ide_plugins` tool (`utils/server/tool-handlers.mjs:1212-1216`) calls `aggregateIdePlugins` (`utils/ide-plugins.mjs:364-607`).
  - It scans the workspace and `.ploinky/repos/*/<agent>/IDE-plugins/*/config.json` (560-577) whether or not the agent is enabled. Duplicates are dropped by agent directory name (425).
  - `config.json` fields: `pluginCategory:"application"`, `location` (e.g. `file-exp:toolbar`), `type`, `presenter`, `dependencies`, `toolbarModal`, `icon`.
  - Settings entries come from the manifest's `ideSettings` (294-360): `pluginKey` `<agent>/<id>`, then `settingsComponent` or `settingsUrl`, then `adminOnly`.
  - `locationOrder` sets the sort order (`utils/pluginUtils.core.js:125-131`).
  - `adminOnly` hides the entry from non-admins: toolbar filter at `web-components/pages/file-exp/file-exp-application-plugins.js:48`, route guards at `main.js:118, 316, 502`, and in the Settings modal (`web-components/modals/settings-modal/settings-agent-model.js:58-67`).
  - Explorer's `applicationPlugins` only works as a deny-list: an entry set to `false` hides a plugin (`pluginUtils.core.js:438-466`).
  - The plugin UI reaches its agent through `getClient('<agent>').callTool` (`LL/IDE-plugins/local-llm-tool-button/components/local-llm-dashboard/local-llm-dashboard.js:40-44`).
- **What a new agent needs to appear the same way:** its repo in Explorer's `repos`, an `enable` entry, `IDE-plugins/<id>/config.json`, manifest `ideSettings`, a unique agent name, and MCP tools for the dashboard.

## 5. The older repos

**llm-runtime** (2026-05-28 to 06-24)
- **Purpose:** role agents (`planning-local`, `relevance`, `language-detection`) sharing one in-container runtime: an MCP server and a proxy mapping port 9000 to MCP 9001, control 9002 and engine 8080.
  - It reads a Ploinky-mounted `/runtime/selected-architecture.json` plus an agent-owned `agent-models.json` (profiles → launcher candidates by priority and required accelerators).
  - Launcher scripts implement `describe`, `prepare`, `start`, `stop`, `status`.
- **Status:** dead. The only real launcher (llama.cpp CPU, in `base-local`) was removed on 06-18 "superseded by default-local-llm"; the remaining agents have only `fake-cpu` launchers, and the manifests use `profiles.ports`, which DS005 now rejects.
- **arm64 / GPU:** its schemas list `nvidia-cuda` and `linux/arm64`, but no GPU launcher was ever written.
- **Reusable:** the launcher `describe` schema (with `chat/embeddings/rerank` capabilities) and the profile/candidate priority model, which fits coder/fast/big.

**local-llm-architectures** (last commit 06-17)
- **Purpose:** a data-only catalog (9 architectures, images, JSON schemas). Ploinky core still consumes it when a manifest sets `llmRuntime.enabled` (`PL/cli/sandbox/docker/llmRuntimeIntegration.js`, `llmArchitectureCatalog.js:12, 374-412`). Hardware detection maps aarch64 to arm64 and probes `nvidia-smi` and `nvidia-ctk` (`hardwareDetection.js:10-17, 89-124`).
- **Status:** the `nvidia-cuda-arm64` entry is marked experimental. It uses `gpus:"all"`, `ipc:"host"` and 8 GB memory, and points at `ghcr.io/ploinky/llm-runtime-nvidia-cuda-arm64:dev`, whose build context does not exist. The CPU Dockerfiles are placeholders (`tail -f /dev/null`).
- **Why it can't be used for GPU:** its policies conflict with today's Box GPU model, which grants the device `ploinky.local/gpu=all` via `containerSecurity.gpu` and rejects `--gpus` and host IPC (`PL/CLAUDE.md:19`).
- **Reusable:** only the hardware probes and the architecture-id naming convention.

**llm-runtime-cpu image**
- **What it is:** Node 24 plus a CPU-only llama.cpp b6412 `llama-server` build and the Hugging Face CLI.
- **arm64:** yes. CI (`publish-llm-runtime-cpu-image.yml`) runs on `ubuntu-24.04-arm` and defaults to `linux/arm64` with tag `cpu-arm64-smoke`. It is still listed as optional (`CIB/README.md:26-28`).
- **Reusable:** the native-arm64 CI runner and the build-from-source recipe. For GB10 it would need a CUDA 13 base and `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=121` (I believe GB10 is sm_121; not checked here).

**Why `local-llms/local-llm` replaced them:** it is one GPU agent that installs and runs its runners itself (llama.cpp, ik_llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM, TabbyAPI, LM Studio), with an admin dashboard, weight download on Run, discovery through a chatCompletions command, and GPU via the CDI grant. However, its image is amd64-only (`CIB/images/local-llm/Dockerfile:43`; CI publishes `linux/amd64`; CUDA 12.8, compute capabilities 86/89). So it cannot use the GPU natively on a DGX Spark, which is the gap `dgx-local-agent` fills.

## Implications for dgx-local-agent

1. **Must declare `endpoints.chatCompletions.command`** with `supportsStream:true` and a large `timeoutMs` (local-llm uses 600000). Without a command, AgentServer runs the Achilles loop, which calls Soul Gateway itself.
2. **Multiple models need only `endpoints.models.command`; no Soul Gateway change.**
   - Use ids without `/`.
   - Return `contextWindow`, `maxOutputTokens`, `supportsTools` and `supportsVision` for each model.
   - The chat handler must dispatch on `request.model`.
   - The list can include only models that are ready: Soul Gateway disables missing ones within about 60 s and ignores an empty list.
3. **Tags need care.**
   - Set `capabilities.tags` (e.g. `["dgx-local"]`) to stay out of `generic-agent`.
   - Per-model predefined tags (`coding`, `reasoning`, `long-context`, `vision`) automatically put models into those tiers; use them on purpose.
   - Putting a model into `fast`/`code`/`plan`/`deep` needs an admin edit in the Soul Gateway Tiers UI. Alternatively, a Soul Gateway change could seed "local-first" tier children automatically.
4. **Reasoning needs a decision.** Soul Gateway strips `reasoning_effort` and `chat_template_kwargs` and drops `reasoning_content`. Either fix thinking behaviour per model inside the agent (e.g. `coder` without thinking, `big` with it), or patch `ploinky-agent-openai.backend.mjs` around line 596 to:
   - send a keep-alive during `delta.reasoning_content` / `delta.reasoning`;
   - forward more fields (or use the provider's `settings.extra_body`).
5. **Long contexts need longer timeouts.** Raise the Soul Gateway per-model `requestTimeoutMs` (default 120 s) so prefill of 100k+ tokens fits, and have the agent send `usage` in its last SSE chunk, since `stream_options` is not forwarded.
6. **Anthropic `/v1/messages` already works through the gateway**, using model `dgx-local/dgx-local-agent/coder`. A native agent endpoint would need changes in AgentServer, the Router's delegation surface and a new Soul Gateway backend. The alternative, an `httpRoutes` side door, bypasses the gateway's policies and logging.
7. **Embeddings and rerank need changes in four places:** a new manifest endpoint kind, an AgentServer route, a Router delegation surface, and `embed()` in the agent backend. The workaround is a manually configured `openai-api` provider.
8. **Explorer setup:**
   - Add the repo to Explorer's `repos` and `"<repo>/dgx-local-agent no-wait"` to `enable`.
   - Add IDE plugins with unique `id`s, `adminOnly:true` and a `locationOrder`, plus `ideSettings` with pluginKey `dgx-local-agent/<id>`.
   - Consider not enabling `local-llm` by default on arm64 hosts. I haven't checked how its amd64 image fails there.
9. **Build:** an arm64 + CUDA 13 image, reusing the arm64 CI runner pattern from `llm-runtime-cpu`. Request the GPU with `containerSecurity.gpu` plus `shmSize`, not the `llmRuntime` `gpus`/`ipc` policy.</result>

  - Gateway models appear as `soul_gateway/<key>` (`providers/modelsConfigLoader.mjs:532-610`).
  - Per-process override: `LLM_MODELS_CONFIG_PATH` (620-623). The AdvancedLanguageAgent CLI adds `--model`, `ALA_MODEL`, `--tag` and `--model-config`.
- **The tiers themselves live in Soul Gateway.** `fast, code, plan, write, deep, ultra, web-assist` are cascades seeded once from free OpenRouter models (`bootstrap/free-model-catalog.mjs:167-240`; `LLM_DEFAULT_TIERS` at `manifest.json:84`).
- **How tags interact with tiers.**
  - Agent tags are kept as-is; the tag classifier is skipped for discovered agents (`runtime/policy/model-metadata-classifier.mjs:614-615, 643`).
  - Every predefined tag (49-78) except the public tier names (`bootstrap/reconcile-tag-tiers.mjs:10-13`) is an automatic tier. Agent models join it, and for agent providers the tier is created if missing (`reconcile-tag-tiers.mjs:261-330`; `auto-provisioner.mjs:701-709`).
  - `generic-agent` is one of these tags, so every agent without `capabilities.tags` lands in the `generic-agent` cascade.
  - `local-llm` is not a predefined tag. local-llm therefore joins no tier and is reachable only by its explicit id.
- **Mapping `fast` or `code` to a local model: yes, but it is manual.** Public tiers are never filled from tags. An admin edits the tier's children in the Soul Gateway dashboard (Explorer Settings → "Soul Gateway") or via the `/management/tiers` API (`management/tiers-route.mjs:1-17`; `dashboard/js/app.mjs:2636-2808`). - **local-llm is enabled by default.** `EXP/manifest.json:11-29` lists `"local-llms/local-llm no-wait"` (28) and `"proxies/soul-gateway no-wait"` (24), and `repos.local-llms` clones the repo (30-35).
- **How plugins are loaded.** The `collect_ide_plugins` tool (`utils/server/tool-handlers.mjs:1212-1216`) calls `aggregateIdePlugins` (`utils/ide-plugins.mjs:364-607`).
  - It scans the workspace and `.ploinky/repos/*/<agent>/IDE-plugins/*/config.json` (560-577) whether or not the agent is enabled. Duplicates are dropped by agent directory name (425).
  - `config.json` fields: `pluginCategory:"application"`, `location` (e.g. `file-exp:toolbar`), `type`, `presenter`, `dependencies`, `toolbarModal`, `icon`.
  - Settings entries come from the manifest's `ideSettings` (294-360): `pluginKey` `<agent>/<id>`, then `settingsComponent` or `settingsUrl`, then `adminOnly`.

## 5. The older repos

**llm-runtime** (2026-05-28 to 06-24)
- **Purpose:** role agents (`planning-local`, `relevance`, `language-detection`) sharing one in-container runtime: an MCP server and a proxy mapping port 9000 to MCP 9001, control 9002 and engine 8080.
  - It reads a Ploinky-mounted `/runtime/selected-architecture.json` plus an agent-owned `agent-models.json` (profiles → launcher candidates by priority and required accelerators).
  - Launcher scripts implement `describe`, `prepare`, `start`, `stop`, `status`.
- **Status:** dead. The only real launcher (llama.cpp CPU, in `base-local`) was removed on 06-18 "superseded by default-local-llm"; the remaining agents have only `fake-cpu` launchers, and the manifests use `profiles.ports`, which DS005 now rejects.
- **arm64 / GPU:** its schemas list `nvidia-cuda` and `linux/arm64`, but no GPU launcher was ever written.
- **Reusable:** the launcher `describe` schema (with `chat/embeddings/rerank` capabilities) and the profile/candidate priority model, which fits coder/fast/big.

**local-llm-architectures** (last commit 06-17)
- **Purpose:** a data-only catalog (9 architectures, images, JSON schemas). Ploinky core still consumes it when a manifest sets `llmRuntime.enabled` (`PL/cli/sandbox/docker/llmRuntimeIntegration.js`, `llmArchitectureCatalog.js:12, 374-412`). Hardware detection maps aarch64 to arm64 and probes `nvidia-smi` and `nvidia-ctk` (`hardwareDetection.js:10-17, 89-124`).
- **Status:** the `nvidia-cuda-arm64` entry is marked experimental. It uses `gpus:"all"`, `ipc:"host"` and 8 GB memory, and points at `ghcr.io/ploinky/llm-runtime-nvidia-cuda-arm64:dev`, whose build context does not exist. The CPU Dockerfiles are placeholders (`tail -f /dev/null`).

- **Reusable:** only the hardware probes and the architecture-id naming convention.

**llm-runtime-cpu image**
- **What it is:** Node 24 plus a CPU-only llama.cpp b6412 `llama-server` build and the Hugging Face CLI.
- **arm64:** yes. CI (`publish-llm-runtime-cpu-image.yml`) runs on `ubuntu-24.04-arm` and defaults to `linux/arm64` with tag `cpu-arm64-smoke`. It is still listed as optional (`CIB/README.md:26-28`).

However, its image is amd64-only (`CIB/images/local-llm/Dockerfile:43`; CI publishes `linux/amd64`; CUDA 12.8, compute capabilities 86/89). So it cannot use the GPU natively on a DGX Spark, which is the gap `dgx-local-agent` fills.

## Implications for dgx-local-agent

1. **Must declare `endpoints.chatCompletions.command`** with `supportsStream:true` and a large `timeoutMs` (local-llm uses 600000). Without a command, AgentServer runs the Achilles loop, which calls Soul Gateway itself.
2. **Multiple models need only `endpoints.models.command`; no Soul Gateway change.**
   - Use ids without `/`.
   - Return `contextWindow`, `maxOutputTokens`, `supportsTools` and `supportsVision` for each model.
   - The chat handler must dispatch on `request.model`.
   - The list can include only models that are ready: Soul Gateway disables missing ones within about 60 s and ignores an empty list.
3. **Tags need care.**
   - Set `capabilities.tags` (e.g. `["dgx-local"]`) to stay out of `generic-agent`.
   - Per-model predefined tags (`coding`, `reasoning`, `long-context`, `vision`) automatically put models into those tiers; use them on purpose.
   - Putting a model into `fast`/`code`/`plan`/`deep` needs an admin edit in the Soul Gateway Tiers UI. Alternatively, a Soul Gateway change could seed "local-first" tier children automatically.
4. **Reasoning needs a decision.** Soul Gateway strips `reasoning_effort` and `chat_template_kwargs` and drops `reasoning_content`. Either fix thinking behaviour per model inside the agent (e.g. `coder` without thinking, `big` with it), or patch `ploinky-agent-openai.backend.mjs` around line 596 to:
   - send a keep-alive during `delta.reasoning_content` / `delta.reasoning`;
   - forward more fields (or use the provider's `settings.extra_body`).
5. **Long contexts need longer timeouts.** Raise the Soul Gateway per-model `requestTimeoutMs` (default 120 s) so prefill of 100k+ tokens fits, and have the agent send `usage` in its last SSE chunk, since `stream_options` is not forwarded.
6. **Anthropic `/v1/messages` already works through the gateway**, using model `dgx-local/dgx-local-agent/coder`. A native agent endpoint would need changes in AgentServer, the Router's delegation surface and a new Soul Gateway backend. The alternative, an `httpRoutes` side door, bypasses the gateway's policies and logging.

input.title: Make local-llm admission fail closed on N/A GPU memory
input.tldr: While planning a DGX Spark agent, we found that local-llm's admission silently approves every model when nvidia-smi reports memory as [N/A] (as on GB10): the values become NaN and every size check passes. The new session will make the hardware snapshot treat non-finite GPU memory as unknown and refuse runs instead.
input.prompt:
In the local-llms repo at /home/research/work/.ploinky/repos/local-llms, the GPU agent `local-llm` has a fail-open admission bug.

Problem: `readGpu` in `local-llm/src/controller/hardware.mjs` (~lines 50-66) parses `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total,memory.used,memory.free,driver_version --format=csv,noheader,nounits` and does `Number(total) * MIB` etc. On NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark, unified memory) nvidia-smi returns `[N/A]` for all three memory fields, so totalBytes/usedBytes/freeBytes become NaN while `available: true`. Every comparison against NaN in `local-llm/src/controller/admission.mjs` is false, so admission returns `ok` for any model (verified: a fabricated 500 GiB GGUF and a 300 GiB vLLM snapshot were both admitted against a live GB10 snapshot). vLLM then fails later at launch because `--gpu-memory-utilization` is NaN (`src/runners/vllm.mjs` ~line 116 throws invalid_launch). The dashboard (`IDE-plugins/local-llm-tool-button/components/local-llm-dashboard/local-llm-dashboard-view.js` ~lines 63-71 and 350-357) also renders NaN.

Fix: in `readGpu`, if any memory value is not a finite number, return `{ available: false, reason: '...' }` naming that the GPU does not report dedicated memory (unified-memory GPUs such as GB10 are not supported by this agent's admission model), so every Run is refused as `incompatible` with a clear reason. Additionally make admission defensive: any non-finite estimate or capacity input should yield `incompatible`, never `ok`. Add tests in `local-llm/tests/` (node:test) with an `[N/A]` nvidia-smi fixture covering readGpu and admit() for llama.cpp and vLLM. Update `local-llm/docs/specs/DS003-gpu-and-resources.md` to record the rule. Run tests from the repo root with `node --test 'local-llm/tests/*.test.mjs'`. Follow the repo's CLAUDE.md: no AI co-author trailers in commits, no `codex/` branch prefix; do not commit unless asked.
